For those of you who don’t know, I’ve been writing for a long time. While in college, I worked as a freelance journalist and that was one of the jobs I did to support myself and, eventually, my family. I also worked as a stripper. No, not that kind of stripper, I worked as a stripper cleaning wax off floors and putting wax back down on the floors. It was not very exciting.

What story am I going to tell you today? I’m going to tell you how I became a mathematician. More accurately, I’m going to tell you the turning point – the point at which I understood. The point at which I became enlightened into the ways of mathematics.

My mother hatched a young Buddha in the year of our Lord 1957. It was a very short year, at least for me. I was almost born in 1958. I doubt that would have made a difference.

I was a hellion. No, really. See, a friend and I burned his dad’s garage down because his dad wouldn’t let use take his Thunderbird out on the weekend. Never mind that neither of us was old enough to drive, nor really very good at it, we’d decided we wanted to take out that car – and cruise for chicks.

Our request was denied, a fire was set, and much mayhem ensued. In our defense, it was a glorious fire.

So, my father was a career Marine. He was not a violent man and he didn’t spank me – or even ground me. No, he decided that I was off to a military academy. They sent me out for a bunch of tests and, truthfully, that’s something they probably shouldn’t have done.

See, I take tests very well. I’m good at taking tests. I did very, very well on these tests and the parental units were proud.

The Vietnam war was still raging and on the nightly news. (My dad largely coached the USMC softball team.) My mother really, really didn’t want me to go to a military school and so she somehow managed to get me into a very prestigious school called Kents Hill. Kents Hill was one of the first private prep schools in the United States and, yes, it lacks an apostrophe.

I presume they are well aware of the missing apostrophe. I can’t say that I’ve ever asked about it.

Either way, that was my first exposure to the lovely State of Maine. It was a very nice school, located atop a hill, in very rural New England. You can Google it, if you want.

There, I had great math instructions from a man named Mr. Fitch. I didn’t realize it was great instruction until much later. I didn’t realize that I was getting a solid foundation. In fact, I absolutely hated math and I was not very good at it.

One day, I’m sitting there and puzzling over the difficult work of finding the area of some right triangles. I was not doing well, for I was not a bright child. As I said, I test well – that doesn’t actually mean I’m intelligent. These right triangles were kicking my ass.

Mr. Fitch is still alive and I have spoken with him and he’s okay with me using his real last name. Mr. Fitch was a brilliant man, and quite adept at making things understandable.

As I puzzled, pondered, poked, and struggled over the right triangles and their mysterious areas, he had quietly watched me from behind.

And, I remember this moment oh so very well, so very well indeed.

Mr. Fitch spoke, “You know, David, you can just square those, find the area, and divide the result in half.”

That was it… That was my moment of enlightenment! It was at that moment in time that I realized those squiggly lines and moronic symbols were a language. It was then that I realized that mathematics was a language and that it was telling me what to do. It was telling me what the problem was and that I needed to figure out how to answer it.

Importantly, it also was the moment when I realized that there were many ways to potentially say the same thing. Sure, I’d already learned about reducing and making elegant. But, those were pointless exercises to me. They didn’t mean anything so I didn’t care – I didn’t connect any dots.

It was that moment in time that I realized that I could approach mathematics in an understandable fashion. After all, I’d already been taking Latin for years. What’s another language?

I wasn’t immediately good. I wasn’t a promise child. I wasn’t even spectacularly gifted. Not at all – in fact, my maths skills still sucked. They’d continue to suck and I’d continue to struggle.

It never came easy. It was never a magical moment of understanding the math – but lots of individual magical moments where I understood a concept. It was that I’d learned to read the language and think about the domain that it applies to.

If I could give all of you one thing, it would be your own personal Mr. Fitch. He’s still alive and I spoke with him this morning. He was very excited to hear that I’d created a forum for the discussion of math. In fact, he said, “It’s about damned time you got back into it.”

Anyhow, the story continues from here but this is a starting point. It’s a starting point, just as my realization that mathematics was a language was a starting point. It’s the first step on a long and difficult journey of learning, a journey that has no end, a journey that has no destination but continues because that’s the nature of such a trek.

I’ll often repeat, “Mathematics is a language.” It’s easy to say, but actually finding your own personal right triangles, and gain true understanding of this, is not so very simple. If you find your right triangles, cherish that moment. Remember that moment. Understand and reflect on that moment.
